'''''Phragmites karka''''', the '''tall reed''' or '''common reed''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Poaceae|grass family]]. It is native to [[West Africa]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Phragmites karka (Retz.) Trin. ex Steud. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:415942-1 |access-date=2025-02-26 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
This species has a widespread distribution that includes West Africa, Southern Arabian Peninsula, Kenya, South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands.<ref name=":0"/> It is also present in New Zealand, where it is categorised as an invasive weed.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |date=26 August 2024 |title=List of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024 |url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/sfc340.pdf |journal=New Zealand Government}}</ref>

== Description ==
It is a herbaceous, perennial species with a rhizomatous [[geophyte]] (underground storage organ) and primarily grows in the tropical regions during the dry season. During the winter, it is deciduous.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Phragmites karka |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/phragmites-karka/ |access-date=2025-02-26 |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |language=en}}</ref>

Plants can grow to 4–10 metres in height, with a diameter of 15-25mm.<ref name=":1" /> 
[[File:Phragmites karka 188653184.jpg|thumb|Interior of a tall reed stem]]

The species is a fast-growing aquatic plant, often found in swamps, riverbanks and standing water, usually at elevations below 1,000 m.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Phragmites karka - Useful Tropical Plants |url=https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Phragmites+karka |access-date=2025-02-26 |website=tropical.theferns.info}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Tall Reed (Phragmites karka) |url=https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/166742-Phragmites-karka |access-date=2025-02-26 |website=iNaturalist |language=en}}</ref>

== Uses ==
Locally, this species is utilised as a source of building and construction material, and as food. It is often planted near rivers to purify water, and as an anchor against soil erosion.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> The young shoots of this plant can be cooked and eaten, like bamboo or asparagus. The young leaves can also be used as fodder.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> The grass is also use for thatching and making screens, baskets, brooms, hats, mats, paper and reeds for musical instruments and fuel.<ref name=":2" />

In the Philippines, the [[panicle]]s of this species are bunched-up in a fan-shape to create a broom, with the culms being tightly bound to a central bamboo piece.<ref>{{Cite book |last=W. H. |first=Brown. |title=Minor Products of Philippine Forests |date=1920 |publisher=Bureau of Forestry, Manilla}}</ref>

== Conservation ==
This widespread, fast-growing species is classified by the IUCN as Least Concern.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Richard Lansdown (Aquatic Plant Expert) |last2=Fatima Niang Diop (Institut des Sciences de l'Environnement, Universite Cheikh Anta Diop de Dakar, Senegal) |date=2019-09-29 |title=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species: Phragmites karka |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/168955/140441144 |journal=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250120100845/https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/168955/140441144 |archive-date=2025-01-20}}</ref>
